summary:
Mexico has no national administrative procedure for legal gender recognition; the process is set state by state. As of March 2025, 22 of the 32 states had legislated an administrative recognition procedure, two more operated one in practice without legislative enactment, and six state legislatures had enacted none. Only seven states extend recognition to children. A trans visitor's legal position therefore depends on which state they are in.

In 2022 the Supreme Court set binding guidelines for the states and extended the right to minors, and the Inter-American Court of Human Rights requires a simple, accessible procedure. Six state legislatures have still enacted none.

Where no procedure exists, identity-document mismatch drives discrimination in schools, medical clinics and the labour market, with incidents recorded in Guanajuato and Tabasco.

Tabasco has no legal gender-recognition procedure. Without identity documents matching a trans person's gender, every document request or appearance scrutiny carries risk of violence, harassment and humiliation, and trans people are excluded from employment, health services, education and financial transactions.

Violence against trans people in that state is documented: trans woman Karina Gomez was murdered in Villahermosa in August 2023. Nationally, more than 95% of homicides went unpunished in 2022.

Partner recognition is settled nationwide. By 31 December 2022 every state had legalised marriage for same-sex couples by legislation, executive order or judicial ruling, though only twenty states allow those couples to adopt children. Civil unions are performed in Campeche, Coahuila, Mexico City, Michoacan, Sinaloa, Tlaxcala and Veracruz.

Protection machinery exists on paper. A federal anti-discrimination law took effect on 11 June 2003, creating a national council to enforce it. Article 1 of the Federal Constitution was amended in 2001 to prohibit discrimination under the term "preferences", and in June 2011 the more precise term "sexual orientation" was inserted. Mexico City banned discrimination based on sexual orientation on 2 September 1999, the first such ordinance in the country.
tangentialFactors:
Recognition regimes differ sharply between states. Mexico City has operated a procedure since 2004, while Tabasco has none, so a visitor's legal position changes at state lines.

In the Isthmus of Tehuantepec, Zapotec communities recognise a traditional third gender, the muxe, intermediate between male and female. Muxes are assigned male at birth and do both women's and men's work, and having a muxe in the family is regarded as good luck. The source describes them as neither devalued nor discriminated against within their communities, while noting that mestizo police occasionally harass and persecute muxe boys and that Zapotec parents, especially mothers, defend them.
localsOnly:
Mexico City amended its Civil Code with effect from 13 March 2004 to allow transgender people to change gender and name on birth certificates. In September 2008 its Legislative Assembly passed a law making the change easier, and on 13 November 2014 it approved a gender identity law that made the process quicker and simpler. In late August 2008 the legislature passed 37-17 a law formalising the procedure for name changes and revised birth certificates reflecting gender identity, replacing a prior process without specific rules that could take years in court.

Gender identity laws followed in Michoacan on 13 July 2017, Nayarit on 20 July 2017, Coahuila on 13 November 2018, Hidalgo on 25 April 2019, and San Luis Potosi began authorising legal gender changes on 17 May 2019. On 17 October 2018 the Supreme Court held that a transgender person could change name and gender marker on official documents through a simple administrative process based solely on their own declaration of gender identity.

Mexico City legalised marriage for same-sex couples on 21 December 2009, effective 4 March 2010, and the Supreme Court upheld its constitutionality on 5 August 2010 by 9 to 2. On 3 June 2015 the Court released a jurisprudential thesis deeming laws restricting marriage to a man and a woman unconstitutional and requiring every judge to validate same-sex unions through amparo, with a nationwide adoption jurisprudence finalised on 23 September 2016. By 31 December 2022 every state had legalised same-sex marriage by legislation, executive order or judicial ruling, though only twenty allowed those couples to adopt children. Civil unions for same-sex and opposite-sex couples are performed in Campeche, Coahuila, Mexico City, Michoacan, Sinaloa, Tlaxcala and Veracruz.
outOfScopeNotes:
The 95% impunity figure is a 2022 national homicide statistic, not specific to trans people, and the sources do not provide prosecution rates for violence against trans people.

The sources describe anti-discrimination protection in terms of sexual orientation; whether the 2003 federal law and the constitutional amendment cover gender identity is not established.

The account of the muxe is ethnographic and describes social practice rather than legal protection; how police treatment of muxe people is handled under the law is not sourced.

Whether the six states without any recognition procedure have pending legislation is not sourced.
